A.explanation: This uses the original unextended diameter of $1.5\text{ cm}$, giving $\sigma \approx 2.1 \times 10^6\text{ Pa}$. It is the minimum stress, not the maximum stress at the neck.

B.explanation: This value is too small because it uses too large a cross-sectional area. It does not use the $0.60\text{ cm}$ minimum diameter where stress is greatest.

C.explanation: This value is too small because it does not correctly use $A = \pi d^2/4$ with $d = 0.60\text{ cm}$ for the narrowest section.

D.explanation: Using the smallest area from $d = 0.60\text{ cm}$, $\sigma = F/A = 363 / (\pi \times 0.0030^2) \approx 1.3 \times 10^7\text{ Pa}$.

hints: Notice the extended rod necks to a minimum diameter of $0.60\text{ cm}$, much smaller than the original $1.5\text{ cm}$.
Recall tensile stress is $\sigma = F/A$ with $A = \pi d^2/4$, so for the same $363\text{ N}$ force the stress is largest where the area is smallest.
Convert the $0.60\text{ cm}$ diameter to metres, calculate the neck area, then divide $363\text{ N}$ by that smallest area.
walkthrough: Identify the governing idea: tensile stress is $\sigma = F/A$, where $F$ is the applied force and $A$ is the cross-sectional area at that position.
Maximum stress occurs at minimum area. From the diagram this is the neck where diameter is $d = 0.60\text{ cm} = 0.0060\text{ m}$, not the original $1.5\text{ cm}$.
Calculate the neck radius $r = d/2 = 0.0030\text{ m}$ and area $A = \pi r^2 = \pi \times (0.0030)^2 \approx 2.83 \times 10^{-5}\text{ m}^2$.
Check units: $\text{N m}^{-2} = \text{Pa}$, and round to two significant figures as in the options to give $1.3 \times 10^7\text{ Pa}$. This is option D.
